deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a page of Riemann's posthumously published essay 'Mechanik des Ohres' (edited by Henle, Zeitschrift für rationelle Medicin, 3. Reihe, Bd. 29, 1867; reprinted in the Gesammelte Werke). The image shows printed text, not a manuscript hand. The content is qualitative physiological mechanics, continuing section V, which asks which forces hold the ossicles in their correct position.

(1) Method. Riemann admits he cannot obtain anatomical data on the elasticity and tension of the ligaments and membranes in fresh preparations. He therefore proposes to work out the consequences of each rival hypothesis and to discard those that lead to improbabilities. This is a hypothetico-deductive exclusion argument.

(2) Two distinctions are introduced: the 'listening' ear (lauschendes Ohr, adapted for exact hearing) versus the non-listening ear, and, for some questions, the newborn's ear versus the adult's.
- The listening state is defined as follows. Pull of the M. tensor tympani presses the stapes footplate slightly against the labyrinth fluid. In modern terms, p_labyrinth = p_tympanic-air + δ with small δ > 0.
- In this state the solid parts whose contact must be secured are pressed slightly against each other.

(3) Concession to sceptics. Those who find such a permanent preload of the apparatus implausible (the tympanic membrane perhaps excepted) may assume something else. Under temperature changes, the ossicles would shift position through the ligaments and gradual changes in muscle contraction, without being pressed together.
- Riemann's justification: only with mutual pressure is exact meshing of all parts guaranteed.
- The analysis then remains valid for the deliberately adapted ear. It also leaves open that the waking ear is continuously adapted to a lesser degree.

(4) Kinematic model of the ossicular chain.
- Malleus and incus form one rigid body that rotates about an axis.
- The stapes articulates with this body and acts as a piston on the fluid of the oval (vestibular) window.
- One end of the rotation axis is the short process of the incus, attached by the incus–tympanic joint to the posterior wall of the tympanic cavity.
- The other end is the long (anterior) process of the malleus. Surrounded only by soft tissue, it lies in a fissure between the anterior-superior end of the tympanic ring and the petrous bone, resting in a groove of the ring (stated for the newborn).

(5) Orientation. Henle's convention is introduced for describing positions: imagine the tympanic cavity rotated so that the rotation axis runs horizontally front–back and the oval window is vertical. The sentence is completed on the next page.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible, since there are no computations.

Physiological remark, not an error of reasoning: the definition of the 'listening' state attributes the stapes preload to the tensor tympani alone. Modern physiology views tensor tympani (and stapedius) contraction mainly as stiffening and attenuating the chain (acoustic reflex), not as tuning for acuity. Riemann's adaptation hypothesis is therefore not accepted today.

Riemann himself notes the anatomical description of the long malleal process lying in the fissure holds 'at least for the newborn'. In the adult this process is usually reduced or ankylosed, so the description is restricted, not wrong.

results.what: Malleus and incus treated as one rigid body rotating about a fixed axis through the short incudal process and the anterior (long) malleal process, with the stapes as an articulated piston
results.modern_name: Ossicular axis of rotation (malleus–incus rigid-body/lever model of the middle ear)
results.usually_credited_to: Helmholtz (1868, 'Die Mechanik der Gehörknöchelchen und des Trommelfells'); the anatomical axis was also described by Henle and earlier anatomists

results.what: 'Listening' ear defined by tensor-tympani preload, giving labyrinth pressure slightly above tympanic air pressure and keeping the ossicles in pressed contact
results.modern_name: Middle-ear muscle accommodation hypothesis (preload / static tension of the ossicular chain)
results.usually_credited_to: Discussed by J. Müller, Toynbee, Politzer and others in the 19th century; this specific formulation appears in Riemann's 'Mechanik des Ohres' (1867)

results.what: Methodological principle of excluding hypotheses by deriving their improbable consequences when direct measurement is unavailable
results.usually_credited_to: General scientific method; Riemann states it explicitly in this essay

It contains only qualitative anatomical and physiological reasoning with no mathematics, and its ideas are already attributed to him in the literature.
